Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. Conversely, write
$w=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and $z=p-c(t)$. If $w\times z=0$, choose a
coordinate $i$ with $w_i\neq0$; the cross-product coordinate equations
([[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1) give
$w_i z_j=w_j z_i$ for every $j$, hence $z=(z_i/w_i)w$.
This proves that the zero relative-velocity set is exactly the displayed
line. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), let $\nu$ be a measure on the measurable space
$(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-measure-space]]) that is
**finite** and **bounded**: $\nu(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Put $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in[0,+\infty)$; nonnegativity follows from the
definition of measure [[def-measure]]. If $m>0$, then $\nu$ is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]. If $m=0$, then for every Borel set
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ one has $0\le\nu(E)\le\nu(\mathbb R^3)=0$, so $\nu$ is the zero measure.
Integrals against $\nu$ are Lebesgue integrals as in [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], defined componentwise for
vector- and matrix-valued integrands. When $m>0$, recall that the inertia matrix of $\nu$ is

$$I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$

with $I_3$ the identity matrix and entrywise integrals
$I(\nu)_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$
and the matrix conventions are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
[[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

**Shifted integrand and inertia tensor about a point.** For $a\in\mathbb R^3$ define the
component functions

$$G_a(\rho)_{jk}:=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2\,\delta_{jk}-(\rho_j-a_j)(\rho_k-a_k)\qquad(j,k\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

equivalently the matrix-valued function
$G_a(\rho)=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}$, and define the **inertia
tensor of $\nu$ about $a$** $I_\nu(a)\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ by its entries

$$I_\nu(a)_{jk}:=\int G_a(\rho)_{jk}\,d\nu(\rho).$$

Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) each entry is
a finite real number; this is the content of [[lem-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point-is-finite]],
which depends on this definition only for its notation. For $a=0$ the shifted integrand is the
parent integrand $\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}$. Thus
$I_\nu(0)=I(\nu)$ when $m>0$; if $m=0$, the parent definition does not define $I(\nu)$, while
the shifted integral remains defined and equals the zero matrix $0_{3\times3}$ for every $a$.

**Scope.** The definition names a mathematical function $a\mapsto I_\nu(a)$ from $\mathbb R^3$ to
$M_3(\mathbb R)$ determined by any finite bounded Borel measure $\nu$ and its coordinate origin.
For the zero measure this function is identically $0_{3\times3}$. No physical body, unit system or
measured mass is asserted. No translation identity for nonzero $a$ is asserted here; the centred,
positive-total-mass case is proved separately on this page.

Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

u$ be a measure on $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]) that is finite and bounded: $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $

1. for all $j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ the functions $ho\mapstoho_j$ and $ho\mapstoho_jho_k$ are Borel measurable and $
u$-integrable, with $\int\lvertho_jvert\,d
u\le R\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and $\int\lvertho_jho_kvert\,d
u\le R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$;
2. consequently the total mass $m=
u(\mathbb R^3)$, the first moment $\mu(
u)$ and every entry of the inertia matrix $I(
u)$ of the definition are well-defined finite real numbers, and $\lvert\mu(
u)_jvert\le R\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$ while $\lvert I(
u)_{jk}vert\le 2R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\nu$ be
a measure on $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that is finite and bounded:
$\nu(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some
real $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let $a\in\mathbb R^3$. With the shifted integrands
$G_a(\rho)_{jk}=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-(\rho_j-a_j)(\rho_k-a_k)$ of
[[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]] ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]] for the norm), then:

1. for all $j,k$ the function $G_a(\cdot)_{jk}:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is Borel measurable and
   $\nu$-integrable
   ([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]);
2. each entry $I_\nu(a)_{jk}$ is a finite real number and

$$\bigl|I_\nu(a)_{jk}\bigr|\le 2\bigl(R+\lVert a\rVert_2\bigr)^2\,\nu(\mathbb R^3).$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Vectors $u,v$ in an inner product space ([[def-inner-product-space]]) are **orthogonal**, written $u\perp v$, if $\langle u,v\rangle=0$. Two subspaces are orthogonal if every vector in one is orthogonal to every vector in the other.

A list or set of vectors is **orthogonal** if every two distinct members are orthogonal. It is **orthonormal** if it is orthogonal and every member has induced norm ([[def-inner-product-norm]]) equal to $1$. An **orthonormal basis** is an ordered basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) that is an orthonormal list.

The empty list is orthonormal and is the orthonormal basis of the zero space. A one-element list is orthogonal; it is orthonormal exactly when its vector has norm $1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $(V,\tau,g,A)$ be as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] and let $(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ and $(o',u',(e_1',e_2',e_3'))$ be two adapted charts, with coordinate functions $(t,x)$ and $(t',x')$ of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]].

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,v\in\mathbb R^3$ and a matrix $R\in O(3)$ such that for every $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a.$$

If $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(e_1',e_2',e_3')$ are both positively oriented for the fixed orientation of $K$, then $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]).

2. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate interval and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a map whose first-chart time coordinate satisfies $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all $s\in I$. Write $x(s):=x(\gamma(s))$ and $y(s):=x'(\gamma(s))$. The regularity hypothesis below means that this coordinate function $x:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuously differentiable (respectively, twice continuously differentiable); no additional smooth structure on $A$ is assumed. If $x$ is continuously differentiable then $y$ is continuously differentiable with

$$y'(s)=R\,x'(s)+v\qquad(s\in I),$$

and if $x$ is twice continuously differentiable then $y''(s)=R\,x''(s)$ for all $s\in I$. Equivalently, in the differentiated variables of the two charts, $dx'/dt'=R\,dx/dt+v$ and $d^2x'/dt'^2=R\,d^2x/dt^2$.

3. Consequently $x''=0$ on $I$ if and only if $y''=0$ on $I$: the two charts agree on which time-parametrized curves have zero coordinate acceleration.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about frames, in the spacetime structure of [[post-cm01-spacetime]].

**(i) Rotations.** A **rotation** is a matrix $R\in SO(3)$, where

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: the time
coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

**(iii) Stationary observers.** For $x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ the curve
$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,
is the **observer at rest in the frame at position $x_{0}$**; the family
$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$. Here an **observer
worldline** means precisely a $C^2$ curve $\alpha:I\to A$ on a nondegenerate
open real interval with $t(\alpha(s))=s$, used to describe an observer; the
stationary curves just defined have $I=\mathbb R$. This kinematic definition
assigns neither a particle label nor a mass or a dynamical law to an observer.
A particle worldline will separately be assigned to a particle label in the
particle postulate. The congruence is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an additional primitive. Distinct frames can have the same family of parametrized curves: if $o' = o+\sum_jc_je_j$ while $u'=u$ and $e_j'=e_j$, then $\alpha'_{x_0}(t)=\alpha_{x_0+c}(t)$ for all $t$. Thus shifting only the spatial origin relabels this family. Changing $u$ changes the curve family, since every curve in it has the affine derivative $u$.

**(iv) Allowed changes between frames.** The model adopts the class of
transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. Uniqueness follows by comparing the coordinate maps on all $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$: evaluating the time map fixes $b$; evaluating the spatial map at $(0,0)$ fixes $a$, at $(1,0)$ fixes $v$, and at $(0,e_j)$ for the three standard coordinate vectors fixes each column of $R$. The kinematic
consequences of the law — the transformation of coordinate velocity and
acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(v) Free motion is not asserted here.** The framework's dynamics enters
through the force and equation-of-motion postulates of the pages that follow;
those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

**(vi) Kinematic symmetry is not conservation.** The class (iv) is a class of
coordinate changes. A quantity is **conserved along a motion** when its value as a function of the frame time is constant on the interval of that motion. No such constancy is asserted here, nor is it asserted that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and
an external apparatus or background field can single out frames for the
description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

In the notation of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]:

1. $I_3\in SO(3)$, and for all $R,S\in SO(3)$ the matrices $RS$ and $R^{\mathsf T}$ again lie in $SO(3)$; moreover $\det R=1$, $R$ is invertible, and its inverse is $R^{\mathsf T}$, so also $RR^{\mathsf T}=I_3$.
2. Consequently $SO(3)$ is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]).

Let $M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the set of $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb R$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), with identity $I_3$ and product as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], transpose $R^{\mathsf T}$ as in [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and determinant $\det R$ as in [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]].

The **orthogonal group** and the **special orthogonal group** are the subsets

$$O(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\},\qquad SO(3):=\{R\in M_3(\mathbb R):R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3\ \text{and}\ \det R=1\}.$$

Equivalently $SO(3)=O(3)\cap\{R:\det R=1\}$. Elements of $SO(3)$ are called **rotations**. The identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with the function space $\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and hence with $\mathbb R^9$ is the one of [[def-matrix-space]]; when $M_3(\mathbb R)$ is regarded as a metric or topological space, this is always the Euclidean metric of that identification.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $X$ be a set.

1. The intersection of every nonempty family of sigma-algebras on $X$ is a
   sigma-algebra on $X$.
2. For every $\mathcal E\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$, the family
   $\Sigma_X(\mathcal E)$ of [[def-generated-sigma-algebra]] is nonempty, and
   $\sigma_X(\mathcal E)$ is the unique smallest sigma-algebra on $X$ containing
   $\mathcal E$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: By [L1], the description of the motion in the second frame is the displayed map $\tilde x$. Substituting $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ at $t=t'-b$ and distributing the matrix product, $$\tilde x(t',\rho)=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a+QR(t'-b)\rho,$$ so $\tilde x=\tilde c+\tilde R\rho$ with $\tilde c$ and $\tilde R$ as in clause 1. This is the first assertion of clause 2.

Material velocity: differentiating $\tilde x(t',\rho)=Qx(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ with the chain rule [L3] gives $\partial_{t'}\tilde x(t',\rho)=Q\partial_tx(t'-b,\rho)+u$, which is the first identity of clause 3. This proves clause 3.

Momentum: by [L5] applied in the second frame, $\tilde P(t')=m\,\frac{d}{dt'}\tilde c(t')$; differentiating the first identity of clause 1 with the chain rule [L3] gives $\frac{d}{dt'}\tilde c(t')=Qc'(t'-b)+u$, where $c'$ is the time derivative of the first-frame path $c$; hence $\tilde P(t')=Q(mc'(t'-b))+mu=QP(t'-b)+mu$ by [L5] in the first frame.

Inertia data: the reference mass distribution of the model is the same data in either frame; hence the body inertia matrix computed from $\nu$ is $I$ in both descriptions. Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $c\in[0,+\infty]$. Define the scalar set function $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches:

$$ (c\mu)(E):=\begin{cases}0,&c=0,\\c\,\mu(E),&0<c<+\infty,\\0,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)=0,\\+\infty,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)>0.\end{cases}$$

Thus neither the zero branch nor the infinite branch forms the undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For measures $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ on the same measurable space and weights $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$, their **countable weighted sum** is the pointwise set function

$$\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\mu_k\right)(E):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(c_k\mu_k)(E),$$

using [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Finite weighted sums are defined by the corresponding finite partial sum, with the empty weighted sum the zero set function. The fact that all these set functions are measures is [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]].

by

they are measurable by

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
